## Abstract

We compare three retrieval strategies over the full 377-paper cBioPortal
cancer-genomics publication corpus. **Agentic** is a language-model agent
that navigates a hand-compiled wiki of papers, genes, cancer types,
datasets, drugs, and methods via six graph-walk tools. **RAG** is standard
dense-vector retrieval: chunk paper markdowns, embed with Vertex AI
`gemini-embedding-001`, pull the top-40 chunks, answer in a single call.
**Hybrid** fuses three retrieval legs — dense vectors, BM25, and a one-hop
walk over the wiki cross-link graph — reranks with a cross-encoder, then
answers in a single call. All three share the answering model
(`claude-haiku-4-5`) and a rubric judge (`claude-opus-4-6`), and crucially
all three search the *same* 377-paper corpus, so the comparison isolates
retrieval strategy from corpus size. On an 80-question set split 48/16/16
across train/val/test and four categories, **no strategy dominates**: on the
held-out test split accuracy is a near-wash (agentic 4.00,
RAG 3.94, hybrid 3.75), while the agent leads
completeness (3.88 vs 3.25 / 3.00)
and citation recall (0.738 vs 0.701 /
0.619) — a lead concentrated in the enumeration-heavy *list* and
*synthesis* categories, bought with substantially more tokens and wall time.
RAG matches the agent on accuracy and edges it on citation correctness at a
small fraction of the cost; hybrid is the cheapest and fastest but trails on
quality. We read this as evidence that graph-walk retrieval earns its cost
only on multi-document questions, and that for single-fact retrieval a
conventional embedding pipeline is competitive. The apparatus, data, and
source are all reproducible from `eval/`.

## Introduction and background

Retrieval-augmented generation ([Lewis 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)) has become the default
recipe for grounding language-model answers in a knowledge base. The
classic implementation is vector search over fixed-size text chunks
([Karpukhin 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906), [Santhanam 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488)), evaluated on
heterogeneous retrieval benchmarks ([Thakur 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663),
[Muennighoff 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316)) and generation-quality rubrics
([Es 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)). In parallel, two threads have emerged that treat
retrieval as a *behaviour* rather than a single lookup: graph-augmented
retrieval ([Edge 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130), [Gutiérrez 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831),
[Guo 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05779), [Gao 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08815)) builds an explicit
structure over the corpus and walks it; agentic retrieval
([Yao 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629), [Nakano 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332), [Asai 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511),
[Yan 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884), [Singh 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09136)) lets a language-model
agent decide what to read next based on what it just saw. Both converge
on the same observation: for questions that span documents, flat top-k
vector search is **not the best fit**.

This study evaluates that proposition for a cancer-genomics knowledge base
that powers a conversational question-answering interface. We maintain a
hand-compiled wiki of papers, genes, cancer types, datasets, drugs, and
methods (377 papers in this study, a subset of the cBioPortal publication
list together with related work), cross-linked between entity pages and their
citing papers. The central question is whether, given that graph, an agent
that walks it outperforms a conventional dense-RAG pipeline — or a hybrid that
augments dense retrieval with BM25 and a one-hop graph expansion — over the
same papers. A positive result would justify investing in richer structure in
the knowledge base; a negative one would indicate that the structure does not
earn its keep and that a plain embedding pipeline suffices. Following the
tradition of biomedical question-answering evaluation, we use a language model
to author a question set spanning four categories — *lookup* (single-paper
factoid), *list*, *synthesis*, and *definition* ([Krithara 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02068-4),
[Jin 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06146), [Wadden 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974)).

Several aspects of the setup are deliberately simple. The wiki graph has no
community-detection layer ([Edge 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)), no pre-computed theme or
subgraph summaries, and no adaptive retrieval loop ([Asai 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511),
[Yan 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884)); the choice of what to abstract from each paper, and what
to treat as an entity, has not been systematically optimized. Because the
question set is language-model-authored with limited manual review, the
absolute scores should be read as indicative rather than definitive, and the
relative comparison across modes is the object of interest.

## Methods

**Corpus.** 377 papers from the cBioPortal publication list, selected because
they were fully ingested into both the compiled wiki (at
`wiki/papers/{pmid}.md`) and the chunking/embedding pipeline (raw markdown
at `data/raw/papers/{pmid}.md`). All three retrieval modes index exactly this
set, with no side channel. Sharing a single corpus across modes is a
deliberate control: it ensures the measured differences reflect retrieval
strategy rather than differences in corpus coverage.

**Question set.** 80 questions authored by an LLM, split 48 / 16 / 16 across
train / val / test, and tagged with one of four categories: *lookup*
(single-paper factoid, 27), *list* (enumerate papers or entities meeting a
criterion, 10), *synthesis* (cross-paper claim, 25), or *definition* (what is
X?, 18). Each question carries one or more gold PMIDs so we can measure
citation recall independently of the judge; *list*-question gold is the
comprehensive expected set over the full 377-paper corpus.

**Agentic mode.** A PydanticAI agent using `claude-haiku-4-5` with six
graph-walk tools: `read_page`, `read_section`, `follow_links`,
`find_references`, `get_page_metadata`, `list_pages`. The system prompt
instructs the agent to start from `index.md` and traverse by title match →
entity pivot → follow links. A hard cap of 20 tool calls per query and a
180-second wall-clock deadline are enforced at the server and runner
layers respectively.

**RAG mode.** Paper markdowns are chunked (~900 chars with 120 overlap),
embedded with Vertex AI `gemini-embedding-001` (3072-dim), and stored in a
FAISS `IndexFlatIP` for cosine similarity. At query time we embed the
question, pull the top-40 passages (budgeted to ~60k characters of
context), and issue a single `claude-haiku-4-5` call with the stitched
passages plus the question.

**Hybrid mode.** Three retrieval legs run over the same index and are fused:
(1) *dense* — the RAG vector leg above; (2) *BM25* — a `rank_bm25.BM25Okapi`
lexical index built from the same chunk `meta.jsonl`; (3) *graph 1-hop* —
entity anchors extracted from the question expand over `wiki/graph.json`
cross-edges to citing papers. Candidates are reranked by a cross-encoder
before being packed into a single `claude-haiku-4-5` call. Hybrid is meant
to combine RAG's lexical/semantic recall with a thin slice of the agent's
graph awareness, without the agent's multi-call traversal cost.

**Judge.** `claude-opus-4-6` reads the question, gold notes, and the
agent's final answer, and returns three integer scores on a 1–5 rubric —
*accuracy*, *completeness*, *citation_correctness* — plus a free-text
reason. We separately compute citation recall as the fraction of gold
PMIDs cited in the answer (detected by regex on `PMID:\d+` and
`papers/\d+\.html` link forms). Full rubric and scoring code are in
[eval/judge.py](https://github.com/jim-bo/cbio-kb/blob/main/eval/judge.py)
and [eval/README.md](https://github.com/jim-bo/cbio-kb/blob/main/eval/README.md).

## Results

### Headline numbers (train split)

Mean scores on the 48-question train split, all three modes. Judge scores
are on a 1–5 scale; citation recall is the fraction of gold PMIDs appearing
in the answer.

| Metric | Agentic | Hybrid | Rag |
|---|---|---|---|
| accuracy (1–5) | 4.04 | 3.85 | 4.21 |
| completeness (1–5) | 3.90 | 3.19 | 3.69 |
| citation correctness (1–5) | 3.60 | 3.64 | 3.85 |
| citation recall vs gold | 0.703 | 0.663 | 0.741 |
| avg wall time (s) | 21.9 | 5.7 | 7.4 |
| avg input tokens | 284230 | 3339 | 11962 |
| avg output tokens | 1093 | 278 | 342 |

*Takeaway — no clean winner. On train, RAG actually leads accuracy, citation
correctness, and citation recall; agentic's only lead is completeness. Hybrid
is by far the cheapest (≈3k input tokens vs RAG's ≈12k and agentic's ≈280k)
and fastest, but trails on every quality metric. The agent's cost — roughly
20–80× the tokens and ~3× the wall time — buys completeness, not accuracy.*

### Figure 1 — Mean judge score by question category

Each category is a different flavour of question. Categories where
*completeness* (did you enumerate the facts?) carries signal are where
the agent's per-page reading pays off — and the only place it clearly leads.

![Figure 1. Mean judge score by question category and mode (agentic / hybrid /
RAG). Each panel is one metric (accuracy / completeness / citation). The
agent pulls ahead only on *completeness* for list and synthesis; elsewhere
RAG is even or better.](plots/category_bars.png)

*Takeaway — the agent's advantage is narrow and category-specific: it leads
completeness on list (≈3.0 vs RAG 2.3) and synthesis (≈3.2 vs 2.6), the
enumeration-heavy categories where full-page reading matters. On lookup and
definition RAG matches or beats it, and on list/synthesis accuracy the agent
actually trails RAG. Hybrid is the weakest on the multi-document categories —
its one-hop graph leg does not recover the agent's completeness edge.*

### Generalization: train / val / test

Three disjoint splits run with identical configuration. We tuned nothing
between splits, so consistency across the three says which differences are
real signal rather than one split's noise.

#### Agentic

| metric | train (n=48) | val (n=16) | test (n=16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| accuracy | 4.04 | 4.38 | 4.00 |
| completeness | 3.90 | 4.12 | 3.88 |
| citation | 3.60 | 3.06 | 3.50 |
| citation recall | 0.703 | 0.616 | 0.738 |
| wall time (s) | 21.9 | 14.9 | 13.9 |

#### Hybrid

| metric | train (n=48) | val (n=16) | test (n=16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| accuracy | 3.85 | 4.00 | 3.75 |
| completeness | 3.19 | 3.38 | 3.00 |
| citation | 3.64 | 3.62 | 3.38 |
| citation recall | 0.663 | 0.744 | 0.619 |
| wall time (s) | 5.7 | 6.4 | 5.7 |

#### Rag

| metric | train (n=48) | val (n=16) | test (n=16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| accuracy | 4.21 | 4.44 | 3.94 |
| completeness | 3.69 | 3.94 | 3.25 |
| citation | 3.85 | 3.62 | 3.69 |
| citation recall | 0.741 | 0.739 | 0.701 |
| wall time (s) | 7.4 | 7.4 | 6.2 |

*Takeaway — the one finding that holds on every split is the agent's
**completeness** lead. Accuracy is a wash that slightly favours RAG (RAG leads
on train and val, dead-even on test), citation correctness favours RAG, and
citation recall is mixed (RAG on train and val, agent on test). No single mode
is ahead on every metric on any split.*

### Figure 2 — Per-question comparison

Each point is one train-split question plotted at its total judge score
(accuracy + completeness + citation, 3–15) for the agentic vs RAG head-to-head
(hybrid is shown in Figures 1 and 3, not this pairwise view). Bubble size is
proportional to whichever mode took longer on that question. Points above the
dashed *y = x* line are agent wins; below are RAG wins.

The four features are dominated by\u003cbr\u003eintratumour-heterogeneity descriptors (features III and IV), which were shown to\u003cbr\u003ecorrelate wi\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 12.3s\u003cbr\u003eBased on the passages provided, the four CT radiomic features that make up the Aerts\u003cbr\u003eprognostic signature trained on the Lung1 dataset are (PMID:24892406):\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Statistics Energy** - describing the overall density of the tumor volume\u003cbr\u003e2. **Shape Compactness** - quantifying how compact the tumor shape is\u003cbr\u003e3. **Grey Level Nonuniformity** - a measure of intratumor heterogeneity\u003cbr\u003e4. **Wavelet Grey Level Nonuniformity HLH** - also describing intratumor heterogeneity\u003cbr\u003eafter decomposing the image in mid-frequencies\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe signature was built on the Lung1 dataset (n=422 NSCLC patients treated at MAASTRO\u003cbr\u003eClinic) and subsequently validated in independent datasets (Lung2, H&amp;N1, and\u003cbr\u003eH&amp;N2). The hypermutated tumors harbored a distinctive mutational signature of\u003cbr\u003eC&gt;T\u002fG&gt;A transitions at CpC and CpT dinucleotides, reflecting TMZ-induced\u003cbr\u003emutagenesis. These tumors also acquired mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes and\u003cbr\u003edriver mutations in the RB and AKT-mTOR pathways that were not present in their initial\u003cbr\u003etumors (PMID:24336570).","\u003cb\u003eL21 \u00b7 lookup\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e In the MSK high-intensity cfDNA sequencing study, in what percentage of patients was at\u003cbr\u003eleast one tumor-derived (biopsy-matched) mutation detected in cfDNA?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 18.6s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll help you find the answer about the MSK high-intensity cfDNA sequencing study.I\u003cbr\u003eneed to search for the MSK high-intensity cfDNA sequencing study. Let me synthesize the findings from these three landmark cfDNA\u003cbr\u003eassay papers:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Summary\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eAcross the corpus&#x27;s cell-free DNA assay-development papers, a **consistent shared\u003cbr\u003erationale** emerges for sequencing matched white-blood-cell (WBC) DNA alongside plasma:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Shared Rationale for WBC Sequencing:**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) masquerades as tumor-derived mutations.** Without matched\u003cbr\u003eWBC sequencing, the vast majority of cfDNA variants are mis-identified as somatic cancer\u003cbr\u003emutations when they actually originate from\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=3 cite=4 \u00b7 6.9s\u003cbr\u003e# Rationale for Matched WBC Sequencing and CH Prevalence\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Shared Rationale\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe key rationale across these papers is to **distinguish tumor-derived mutations from\u003cbr\u003eclonal hematopoiesis (CH) mutations**, which would otherwise be misclassified as\u003cbr\u003etumor-specific variants (PMID:31768066). Since a large proportion of cfDNA fragments\u003cbr\u003eoriginate from hematopoietic cells, CH mutations can confound tumor mutation burden and\u003cbr\u003emutational signature quantification (PMID:31768066). Without WBC matching, CH mutations\u003cbr\u003ein cancer genes like *TP53* could be incorrectly interpreted as tumor-derived, leading to\u003cbr\u003efalse-positive clinical calls (PMID:31768066). Fragment-length analysis combined with WBC\u003cbr\u003epairing provides additional confidence in variant classification (PMID:34145282).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Fraction of cfDNA Calls Attributable to CH\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe fraction of &quot;somatic&quot; cfDNA variants that are actually CH is substantial:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e- *\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS17 \u00b7 Multiple studies\u003cbr\u003efound no correlation between them (PMID:29337640, PMID:35871175), yet both have similar\u003cbr\u003eindividual predictive capacity (PMID:29337640).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Composite Benefit:**\u003cbr\u003eWhen combined, TMB and PD-L1 together provide enhanced predictive power. Patients with\u003cbr\u003ehigh TMB AND PD-L1 positivity showed the highest response rates (~50% durable clinical\u003cbr\u003ebenefit), while those low for both had the lowest (~18%) (PMID:29337640). Similar results\u003cbr\u003eemerged in NSCLC combination therapy (PMID:29657128).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**MSI-H and High TMB:**\u003cbr\u003eBoth MSI-H and TMB-H are recognized as biomarkers for immunotherapy response (PMID:35\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS21 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Across the corpus&#x27;s large clinical sarcoma sequencing studies, what common\u003cbr\u003econclusions emerge about actionable-alteration yield and the dominance of\u003cbr\u003ecopy-number-driven biology, and how do their cohorts and panels differ?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=4 cite=5 \u00b7 180.1s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll help you find the large clinical sarcoma sequencing studies and their\u003cbr\u003econclusions about actionable alterations and copy-number biology. discussions of PD-L1\u002fCD274 combined positive score\u003cbr\u003elimitations as a biomarker.I&#x27;ll now read key papers that discuss PD-L1 CPS\u003cbr\u003elimitations directly.Based on my search across the corpus, here are the **key limitations\u003cbr\u003eof PD-L1\u002fCD274 combined positive score (CPS) as a predictive biomarker** that emerge:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Central Limitation: Context-Dependency\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**PD-L1 CPS does not predict benefit in all treatment contexts.** The most striking\u003cbr\u003eexample is [head-and-neck cancer with reirradiation](papers\u002f38780927.html): PD-L1 CPS\u003cbr\u003e&lt;20 vs. \u226520 showed **no significant difference in PFS or OS** (68.8% vs. 59.2% 1-year\u003cbr\u003ePFS, P=.86) when combined with [nivolumab](drugs\u002fnivolumab.html), despite PD-L1 being\u003cbr\u003epredictive in recurrent\u002fmetastatic HNSCC with single-agent PD-1 blockade. This suggests\u003cbr\u003e**reirradiation may alter the predictive value of PD-L1 CPS**, potentially through\u003cbr\u003eradiation-indu\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=2 cite=1 \u00b7 6.5s\u003cbr\u003e# Limitations of PD-L1 as a Predictive Biomarker\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eBased on the retrieved passages, several key limitations emerge:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Modest Sensitivity and Specificity\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003ePD-L1 expression has **modest sensitivity and specificity** as a predictor of\u003cbr\u003eimmunotherapy response (PMID:29657128). While tumors with higher PD-L1 expression show\u003cbr\u003eimproved outcomes, many PD-L1-positive tumors do not respond to anti-PD-1 therapies, and\u003cbr\u003esome responses occur in PD-L1-negative tumors (PMID:25765070).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Independent of Other Biomarkers\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003ePD-L1 expression does **not correlate with tumor mutation burden (TMB)** or fraction of\u003cbr\u003egenome with copy number alterations (FGA), limiting its combined predictive capacity\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:29337640). When used alone or in combination with TMB, PD-L1 shows only modest\u003cbr\u003epredictive performance (AUC 0.646) (PMID:29337640).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Technical and Biological Heterogeneity\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e- **Staining variation**: Differences\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS12 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What role does clonal hematopoiesis play in interpreting ctDNA or cfDNA findings\u003cbr\u003eaccording to the corpus?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=3 \u00b7 15.1s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search the corpus for information on clonal hematopoiesis and its role in\u003cbr\u003ectDNA\u002fcfDNA interpretation.Let me search more specifically for papers discussing clonal\u003cbr\u003ehematopoiesis and its role in ctDNA\u002fcfDNA interpretation:Based on the corpus, clonal\u003cbr\u003ehematopoiesis (CH) plays a critical but easily overlooked role in ctDNA\u002fcfDNA\u003cbr\u003einterpretation:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Key Role of CH in cfDNA\u002fctDNA Interpretation\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Clonal hematopoiesis creates a major source of confounding variants.** [Razavi et al.\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:31768066)](papers\u002f31768066.html) demonstrated that **without matched\u003cbr\u003ewhite-blood-cell (WBC) sequencing, clonal hematopoiesis variants masquerade as\u003cbr\u003etumor-derived mutations**: 81.6% of cfDNA variants in non-cancer controls and 53.2% in\u003cbr\u003ecancer patients actually originated from CH, not tumors. The canonical CH genes\u003cbr\u003e([DNMT3A](genes\u002fDNMT3A.html), [TET2](genes\u002fTET2.html), [PPM1D](genes\u002fPPM1D.html),\u003cbr\u003e[TP53](genes\u002f\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=2 cite=1 \u00b7 6.0s\u003cbr\u003e# Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis in ctDNA\u002fcfDNA Interpretation\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eClonal hematopoiesis (CH) plays a critical confounding role in interpreting circulating\u003cbr\u003ecell-free DNA (cfDNA) and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) findings:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Primary Challenge: Confounding Somatic Mutations\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eCH represents a major source of false-positive tumor-derived mutations in cfDNA analysis.\u003cbr\u003eThe vast majority of cfDNA mutations originate from hematopoietic cells rather than\u003cbr\u003etumors\u201481.6% in non-cancer controls and 53.2% in cancer patients had features consistent\u003cbr\u003ewith CH (PMID:31768066). This is particularly problematic because CH mutations in genes\u003cbr\u003elike *DNMT3A*, *TET2*, *PPM1D*, and *TP53* are difficult to distinguish from genuine\u003cbr\u003etumor mutations (PMID:31768066, PMID:33106634).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Prevalence and Clinical Impact\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eCH is remarkably common, detected in 89.5% of cancer patients and 83% of non-cancer\u003cbr\u003econtrols in cfDNA analysis\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS22 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e How does the corpus characterize prostate-cancer progression as an evolutionary\u003cbr\u003etrajectory from primary disease through metastatic castration-resistant disease to\u003cbr\u003eneuroendocrine transformation, and which genomic events mark each transition?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=3 cite=2 \u00b7 24.3s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search the corpus for literature on prostate cancer progression, focusing on\u003cbr\u003ethe evolutionary trajectory from primary through metastatic and neuroendocrine stages.Now\u003cbr\u003elet me search for specific papers on prostate cancer progression, neuroendocrine\u003cbr\u003etransformation, and the evolutionary transitions in this disease.Based on my analysis of\u003cbr\u003ethe corpus, here is how prostate cancer progression is characterized as an evolutionary\u003cbr\u003etrajectory across primary through metastatic castration-resistant and neuroendocrine\u003cbr\u003estages:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Evolutionary Trajectory &amp; Genomic Transitions\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Primary \u2192 Metastatic Castration-Sensitive (mCSPC)**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e[mCSPC](papers\u002f32220891.html) is characterized by early clonal events including\u003cbr\u003e[TP53](genes\u002fTP53.html) and [BRCA2](genes\u002fBRCA2.html) alterations, while\u003cbr\u003e[AR](genes\u002fAR.html) amplification\u002fmutations are uncommon at this stage.\u003cbr\u003e[CDK12](genes\u002fCDK12.html) alterations are\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=2 cite=2 \u00b7 11.5s\u003cbr\u003e# Prostate Cancer Evolution: From Primary Disease to Neuroendocrine Transformation\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Overall Evolutionary Model\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe corpus characterizes prostate cancer progression as **divergent clonal evolution**\u003cbr\u003erather than linear progression. The key finding is that castration-resistant\u003cbr\u003eneuroendocrine prostate cancer (CRPC-NE) arises clonally from castration-resistant\u003cbr\u003eadenocarcinoma (CRPC-Adeno) precursors through branching evolution, with selective\u003cbr\u003epressure favoring AR-independent populations (PMID:26855148).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe study evaluated three potential models: linear progression (sequential acquisition of\u003cbr\u003ealterations), independent evolution (parallel distinct clones), and divergent evolution\u003cbr\u003e(genetic diversification with selective pressure). Analysis of serial tumor samples from\u003cbr\u003eindividual patients supported the **divergent model as most parsimonious**\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:26855148).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Genomic Events Marking Transi\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS23 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Across the glioma papers in the corpus, what consistent role do CDKN2A loss, IDH status,\u003cbr\u003eand temozolomide-induced hypermutation play in malignant progression and recurrence, and\u003cbr\u003ehow do tissue versus CSF liquid-biopsy approaches complement each other?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=1 comp=1 cite=1 \u00b7 2.9s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search the corpus for glioma papers and their findings on these specific\u003cbr\u003emolecular and clinical features.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=5 cite=3 \u00b7 7.7s\u003cbr\u003e# CDKN2A Loss, IDH Status, and Hypermutation in Glioma Progression\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Consistent Roles Across Studies\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**CDKN2A Loss:**\u003cbr\u003eCDKN2A loss emerges as a critical driver of malignant progression across glioma subtypes.\u003cbr\u003eIn IDH-mutant tumors, acquired CDKN2A deletions at recurrence associate with increased\u003cbr\u003eproliferating stem-like cells and poor outcomes (PMID:35649412). Notably, this pattern is\u003cbr\u003especific to IDH-mutant tumors\u2014IDH-wildtype tumors typically harbor CDKN2A deletions at\u003cbr\u003einitial presentation (PMID:35649412). Deep deletions (homozygous) predict significantly\u003cbr\u003eshorter overall survival, while monoallelic alterations have minimal impact\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:33765338). CDKN2A loss is associated with shortened survival in lower-grade\u003cbr\u003eastrocytomas independent of IDH status (PMID:31263031).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**IDH Status and Hypermutation:**\u003cbr\u003eTemozolomide-induced hypermutation occurs at different rates across glioma subtypes, wit\u2026"],"legendgroup":"synthesis","marker":{"color":"#E45756","line":{"color":"white","width":1},"opacity":0.75,"size":[29.354999999999997,22.991999999999997,20.555999999999997,27.031,15.411],"symbol":"triangle-up"},"mode":"markers+text","name":"synthesis \u00b7 val","text":["S10","S11","S12","S22","S23"],"textfont":{"color":"#444","size":9},"textposition":"top center","x":[12,6,7,7,12],"y":[13,9,13,9,3],"type":"scatter"},{"hoverinfo":"text","hoverlabel":{"align":"left","bgcolor":"white","font":{"size":11}},"hovertext":["\u003cb\u003eS13 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e How does the corpus address the use of real-world data and NLP to augment structured\u003cbr\u003egenomic data for outcome prediction?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=3 \u00b7 22.0s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll start by checking the index to understand what themes and papers the corpus\u003cbr\u003ecovers on this topic.Now let me search for themes or papers related to real-world data,\u003cbr\u003eNLP, and outcome prediction.Let me search for papers that specifically address real-world\u003cbr\u003edata, NLP, or outcome prediction by checking some recent papers related to these\u003cbr\u003etopics.Let me look for papers that address integrated approaches to outcome prediction\u003cbr\u003ewith genomic data. to create a\u003cbr\u003e&quot;clinicogenomic, harmonized oncologic real-world dataset.&quot; This overcomes a\u003cbr\u003emajor barrier: &quot;The separation of hospital, academic and commercial entities\u003cbr\u003eresponsible for genomic sequencing, radiology, histopathology and electronic health\u003cbr\u003erecord data is a hurdle to integrative analysis.&quot;\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## NLP for Unstructured Data Extraction\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNLP transformer models automatically extract clinical features from unstructured text,\u003cbr\u003eincluding &quot;cancer progression, sites of tumou\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS14 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Beyond breast and ovarian cancer, where does the corpus document BRCA1\u002fBRCA2 alterations\u003cbr\u003eor HR-pathway involvement?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=3 cite=1 \u00b7 12.6s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search the corpus for BRCA1\u002fBRCA2 and HR pathway findings across cancer\u003cbr\u003etypes.The corpus documents **BRCA1\u002fBRCA2 and HR-pathway involvement in many cancer types\u003cbr\u003ebeyond breast and ovarian**. Here are key examples:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Prostate Cancer\u003cbr\u003e[BRCA2](genes\u002fBRCA2.html) is one of the most frequently altered HR genes in metastatic\u003cbr\u003eprostate cancer (mCRPC), occurring in ~7-12% of cases, often as biallelic loss.\u003cbr\u003e[BRCA1](genes\u002fBRCA1.html) and [ATM](genes\u002fATM.html) alterations are also documented.\u003cbr\u003eThese support [PARP inhibitor](drugs\u002folaparib.html) candidacy in this disease.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Pancreatic Cancer (PDAC)\u003cbr\u003ePathogenic germline variants in [BRCA2](genes\u002fBRCA2.html) (3.7%),\u003cbr\u003e[BRCA1](genes\u002fBRCA1.html) (1.8%), [ATM](genes\u002fATM.html) (1.8%), and\u003cbr\u003e[PALB2](genes\u002fPALB2.html) (0.5%) occur in ~10% of patients overall.\u003cbr\u003e[BRCA2](genes\u002fBRCA2.html)-mutant PDAC shows biallelic loss and clinical PARP-inhibitor\u003cbr\u003ebenefit in se\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=1 cite=1 \u00b7 6.0s\u003cbr\u003eBased on the retrieved passages, the corpus documents BRCA1\u002fBRCA2 alterations corpus:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Consistent Findings: DDR\u002fBRCA1\u002fBRCA2 in Aggressive Pediatric and Young-Adult Cancers\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Ewing Sarcoma (Pediatric)**\u003cbr\u003e[EWSR1::FLI1](papers\u002f25186949.html) directly upregulates [BRCA1](genes\u002fBRCA1.html) while\u003cbr\u003eparadoxically **impairing the ATM\u002fATR-mediated DNA damage response**.\u003cbr\u003eEWS::FLI1-transduced embryonic mesenchymal stem cells showed elevated BRCA1 protein but\u003cbr\u003e**increased basal DNA damage, defective phospho-ATM\u002fATR activation, and &gt;2-fold\u003cbr\u003eenhanced sensitivity to etoposide**\u2014defining a model where DDR impairment despite BRCA1\u003cbr\u003eupregulation drives chemosensitivity.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Neuroblastoma (Pediatr\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=2 comp=1 cite=1 \u00b7 6.2s\u003cbr\u003e# DDR and BRCA1\u002fBRCA2 in Aggressive Pediatric\u002fYoung-Adult Cancers\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eBased on the retrieved passages, several consistent findings emerge:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Limited Predictive Value of DDR\u002fBRCA Alterations\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eDDR pathway alterations, including BRCA mutations, do not consistently predict aggressive\u003cbr\u003ephenotypes or therapeutic vulnerability in certain cancer types. In metastatic colorectal\u003cbr\u003ecancer (mCRC), DDR alterations &quot;do not identify a distinct subtype of CRC, predict\u003cbr\u003eplatinum sensitivity, or lead to homologous recombination deficiency,&quot; and PARP\u003cbr\u003einhibitor studies in mCRC have been negative (PMID:32730818).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Complex BRCA Expression Patterns\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eIn Ewing sarcoma, a highly aggressive pediatric malignancy, researchers observed elevated\u003cbr\u003eBRCA1 expression yet &quot;significant defects in DDR,&quot; suggesting that increased\u003cbr\u003eBRCA1 expression alone does not ensure functional DNA damage response (PMID:25186949).\u003cbr\u003eThe presence\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS24 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Across the corpus&#x27;s GI-cancer papers, what differing roles does KRAS play \u2014 as a\u003cbr\u003eprognostic dosage biomarker, a side-specific driver, and a source of acquired resistance\u003cbr\u003e\u2014 and where do the findings converge?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=1 comp=1 cite=1 \u00b7 8.0s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search for GI cancer papers and KRAS findings to map these roles.Now let me\u003cbr\u003esearch for GI cancer papers specifically to identify the distinct roles. Let me check the\u003cbr\u003ecancer_types for GI cancers.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=2 cite=3 \u00b7 10.1s\u003cbr\u003e# KRAS Roles Across GI Cancers: Prognostic Dosage, Allele-Specific Effects, and Resistance\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Prognostic Dosage Biomarker\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eKRAS mutant allele dosage emerges as a critical prognostic feature independent of\u003cbr\u003emutation type. In pancreatic cancer, **KRAS mutant allele dosage gains\u2014observed in ~20%\u003cbr\u003eof KRAS-mutated diploid tumors\u2014correlate with advanced disease and poor outcomes across\u003cbr\u003eall disease stages** (PMID:39753968). Among resectable patients, median OS was\u003cbr\u003esignificantly lower with dosage gains (23 months vs. 32 months; HR = 2.16, p = 0.03), and\u003cbr\u003ethis effect persists in metastatic disease (PMID:39753968). Conversely, **KRAS wild-type\u003cbr\u003etumors associate with significantly better overall survival and early disease onset**\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:39753968).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Allele-Specific Driver Effects\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eDistinct KRAS mutations drive markedly different phenotypes in PDAC:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e- **KRAS^G12R** enriches in early-stage (stage I) d\u2026","\u003cb\u003eS25 \u00b7 synthesis\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Across the corpus&#x27;s cfDNA\u002fctDNA clinical studies, what common utilities of plasma\u003cbr\u003eand CSF liquid biopsy emerge, and how do the approaches differ by the clinical question\u003cbr\u003eand the confounders they must control for?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=4 cite=2 \u00b7 43.4s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search the corpus for liquid biopsy studies, focusing on cfDNA\u002fctDNA and\u003cbr\u003eplasma\u002fCSF approaches.Let me search the corpus more specifically for liquid biopsy and\u003cbr\u003ecfDNA\u002fctDNA studies.Let me search for specific papers I know are in the corpus that focus\u003cbr\u003eon liquid biopsy approaches.Excellent. Let\u003cbr\u003eme synthesize the findings across these studies into a coherent response.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e---\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Plasma cfDNA and CSF Liquid Biopsy: Utilities and Methodological Contrasts\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eAcross the corpus, cfDNA\u002fctDNA clinical studies reveal **convergent utilities** but\u003cbr\u003e**divergent confounder-control strategies** shaped by the clinical question and tissue of\u003cbr\u003eorigin.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Common Utilities**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Detection of tumor-derived mutations de novo or by genotyping.** [High-intensity\u003cbr\u003esequencing](p\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=3 comp=2 cite=2 \u00b7 8.6s\u003cbr\u003e# Plasma vs. CSF Liquid Biopsy: Utilities and Differences\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Key Clinical Utilities\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**CSF-based liquid biopsy** is particularly suited for CNS tumors, where it provides:\u003cbr\u003e- Detection of tumor DNA in 53% of samples from patients with CNS involvement, with zero\u003cbr\u003efalse positives in control samples without CNS disease (PMID:39289779)\u003cbr\u003e- Higher sensitivity for monitoring CNS disease, including leptomeningeal involvement,\u003cbr\u003ecompared to plasma-based approaches (PMID:39289779)\u003cbr\u003e- Tumor enrichment without hematopoietic dilution, allowing detection even at low\u003cbr\u003ecoverage levels due to high ctDNA proportions (PMID:39289779)\u003cbr\u003e- Clinically actionable genetic alterations distributed consistently with tumor-type\u003cbr\u003especific patterns (PMID:39289779)\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Plasma-based liquid biopsy** remains valuable for systemic disease monitoring but shows\u003cbr\u003elimited utility for primary CNS tumors due to the blood-brain barrier It is validated and approved for\u003cbr\u003eclinical use by the New York State Department of Health Clinical Laboratory Evaluation\u003cbr\u003eProgram and is FDA-authorized (PMID:28481359, PMID:35377946).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe panel is designed to detect somatic alterations in cancer, including:\u003cbr\u003e- Sequence mutations (single-nucleotide variants and small insertions\u002fdeletions)\u003cbr\u003e- Copy number alterations (CNAs)\u003cbr\u003e- Select structural rearrangements and fusions\u003cbr\u003e- Promoter mutations (e.g., TERT promoter)\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eIt analyzes protein-coding exons of cancer-associated genes and selected introns of\u003cbr\u003efrequently rearranged genes (PMID:28481359, PMID:33106634).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Main P\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD02 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e Describe each of the four features in the Aerts CT radiomic signature and what aspect of\u003cbr\u003etumor phenotype they capture.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 14.0s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search for information about the Aerts CT radiomic signature.Let me search for\u003cbr\u003einformation about the Aerts CT radiomic signature specifically.Let me search for radiomic\u003cbr\u003esignature papers.Let me search for the methods related to radiomics.Perfect! Let me provide a\u003cbr\u003ecomprehensive answer.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## The Four Features of the Aerts CT Radiomic Signature\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe [Aerts et al. 2014 study](papers\u002f24892406.html) identified a four-feature CT radiomic\u003cbr\u003esignature that predicts overall survival in lung and head-and-neck cancer patients. Here\u003cbr\u003eare the four features and their biological meaning:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### 1. **Statistics Energy** (Feature I)\u003cbr\u003e- **What it captures**: Overall tumor density and intensity distribution in the CT image\u003cbr\u003e- **Phenotype significance**: Measure\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 5.9s\u003cbr\u003e# The Four Features in the Aerts CT Radiomic Signature\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eBased on the passages, here are the four features of the prognostic radiomic signature\u003cbr\u003edeveloped by Aerts et al. (PMID:24892406):\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Statistics Energy** (Feature 1) \u2014 Describes the overall density of the tumor volume,\u003cbr\u003ecapturing intensity characteristics of the tumor.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e2. **Shape Compactness** (Feature 16) \u2014 Quantifies how compact the tumor shape is.\u003cbr\u003ePatients with more compact\u002fspherical tumors had better survival probability.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e3. **Grey Level Nonuniformity** (Feature 48) \u2014 A measure of intratumor heterogeneity.\u003cbr\u003eFeatures describing heterogeneity in the primary tumor were associated with worse\u003cbr\u003esurvival across all validation datasets.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e4. **Wavelet Grey Level Nonuniformity HLH** (Feature Group 4) \u2014 Also describes intratumor\u003cbr\u003eheterogeneity after decomposing the image in mid-frequencies using wavelet analysis.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe signature emphasizes\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD03 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is the PRISSMM NLP curation framework and how is it used in the MSK-CHORD study?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 12.3s\u003cbr\u003eLet me try a broader search:I found it \u2014 there&#x27;s an `nlp-prissmm` page. The study found:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e- **92% overall accuracy** (86% sensitivity, 98% specificity) against a comprehensive NCI\u003cbr\u003epanel reference standard\u003cbr\u003e- 55% of MSK cases were successfully classified; EZB (22%) was the most common subtype\u003cbr\u003e- Restricting to high-confidence predictions (&gt;90% probability) improved accuracy to\u003cbr\u003e96%\u003cbr\u003e- CNA data proved essential\u2014removing it dropped accuracy to 81%, particularly affecting\u003cbr\u003eA53 subtype\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 6.6s\u003cbr\u003e# LymphGen Classification System and Validation\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## What is LymphGen?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eLymphGen is a probabilistic classification algorithm developed by the National Cancer\u003cbr\u003eInstitute that subclassifies diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) into six molecularly\u003cbr\u003edistinct genetic subtypes: MCD, EZB, BN2, N1, ST2, and A53 (PMID:38497151). This system\u003cbr\u003eprovides broader biological heterogeneity classification than the traditional ABC\u002fGCB\u003cbr\u003e(activated B-cell\u002fgerminal center B-cell) paradigm and includes prognostic correlations\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:38497151).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Validation Methodology\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe corpus describes validation of LymphGen on a clinical 400-gene targeted NGS panel\u003cbr\u003e(MSK-IMPACT) used at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Performance on NCI Cohort (filtered to IMPACT genes):**\u003cbr\u003e- Overall accuracy: 92% (86% sensitivity, 98% specificity) (PMID:38497151)\u003cbr\u003e- In the &quot;Core&quot; group (high-confidence cases &gt;90% probability): 96%\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD05 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is the ROBIN consortium, what projects does it run, and which diseases does it cover?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 16.2s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll search for information about the ROBIN consortium in the knowledge base.Let me\u003cbr\u003esearch for ROBIN in the knowledge base.Based on the knowledge base, I have comprehensive\u003cbr\u003einformation about ROBIN. Let me provide you with a detailed answer:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## **ROBIN (Radiation Oncology-Biology Integration Network)**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **What is ROBIN?**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e[ROBIN](papers\u002f41941260.html) is an NIH\u002fNCI-funded **U54 consortium** that integrates\u003cbr\u003emechanistic biological research directly into prospective clinical radiation-therapy (RT)\u003cbr\u003etrials. Its core mission is to bridge the gap between biological discovery and clinical\u003cbr\u003eradiation oncology practice by embedding longitudinal biomarker research into randomized\u003cbr\u003etrials across multiple disease sites.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### **Five Disease-Focused Centers &amp; Their Projects**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eROBIN comprises five U54-funded research centers, each running its own **Molecular\u003cbr\u003eCharacterization Trial (MCT)**:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Oli\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 7.9s\u003cbr\u003e# The ROBIN Consortium\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe **Radiation Oncology-Biology Integration Network (ROBIN)** is an NIH\u002fNCI-funded U54\u003cbr\u003eprogram designed to address critical gaps in radiation oncology by integrating advanced\u003cbr\u003ebiological research, technological innovation, and clinical practice (PMID:41941260). It\u003cbr\u003ewas founded on the vision of Dr. Norman Coleman, who conceptualized radiation as a\u003cbr\u003edynamic &quot;drug&quot; rather than purely a technical tool.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Structure and Projects\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eROBIN comprises **five specialized centers**, each conducting translational programs\u003cbr\u003elinked to clinical Molecular Characterization Trials (MCTs):\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **OligoMET** (University of Maryland Baltimore, Weill Cornell Medicine, Thomas\u003cbr\u003eJefferson University) \u2013 Focuses on metastatic processes in oligometastatic prostate cancer\u003cbr\u003e2. **ImmunoRad** (multi-institutional consortium) \u2013 Studies radiation-immune system\u003cbr\u003einteractions in rectal cancer\u003cbr\u003e3. **GenRad**\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD06 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e How is and\u003cbr\u003emutational signature approaches:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Genetic Variants**: Pathogenic germline or somatic variants in\u003cbr\u003e[BRCA1](genes\u002fBRCA1.html), [BRCA2](genes\u002fBRCA2.html), and other HRD-associated DNA damage\u003cbr\u003erepair (DDR) genes were identified via [MSK-IMPACT](methods\u002fmsk-impact-panel.html)\u003cbr\u003etargeted clinical Risk-Stratification Paper\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eIn the Shah et al. study (PMID:35764743), HRD status in high-grade serous ovarian cancer\u003cbr\u003eis characterized using multiple genomic Now let me get more details from the\u003cbr\u003emain MiMSI paper:## Summary\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**MiMSI** (Multiple Instance learning for MicroSatellite Instability) is a deep learning\u003cbr\u003eclassifier developed at [Memorial Sloan Kettering](papers\u002f39746944.html) that detects\u003cbr\u003emicrosatellite instability (MSI) from [MSK-IMPACT](methods\u002fmsk-impact-panel.html)\u003cbr\u003etargeted sequencing data.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### How it works:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Input**: Per-microsatellite-locus read distributions from targeted NGS (1,755 loci\u003cbr\u003ecovered by MSK-IMPACT)\u003cbr\u003e2. **Architecture**: \u003cbr\u003e   - ResNet-style CNN feature extractor\u003cbr\u003e   - Multiple-instance learning (MIL) pooling (mean or attention-based)\u003cbr\u003e   - Sigmoid classifier with threshold 0.4\u003cbr\u003e3. **Confidence scoring**: 10 random downsampling runs per sample; cases whose 95%\u003cbr\u003econfidence interval crosses the threshold are flagged as indeterminate\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### Performance vs. MSISensor:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eOn\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 6.2s\u003cbr\u003e# MiMSI: Microsatellite Instability Detection\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## What is MiMSI?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eMiMSI (Multiple-Instance MSI) is a deep learning-based computational tool for detecting\u003cbr\u003emicrosatellite instability (MSI) status from next-generation sequencing data\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:39746944). It uses a deep neural network trained with a multiple instance learning\u003cbr\u003eframework, specifically designed to improve MSI detection in challenging cases with low\u003cbr\u003etumor purity\u2014a common issue in routine clinical samples.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## How It Works with MSK-IMPACT Data\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Model Architecture:**\u003cbr\u003e- MiMSI employs a deep convolutional neural network based on ResNet-18 architecture\u003cbr\u003e(adapted to 12 layers) to extract feature embeddings from microsatellite sites\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:39746944)\u003cbr\u003e- The model processes vectorized representations of sequencing reads at microsatellite\u003cbr\u003eloci, incorporating mapping qualities and CIGAR strings\u003cbr\u003e- It generates instance-level embeddings for each\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD12 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is MSK-ACCESS (the ACCESS129 assay), and how does paired normal sequencing improve\u003cbr\u003ecfDNA mutation calling?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 11.9s\u003cbr\u003eI&#x27;ll look up the MSK-ACCESS assay and how paired normal sequencing improves its\u003cbr\u003eperformance.Now let me read the ACCESS129 page for more specific technical details:##\u003cbr\u003eSummary\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**[MSK-ACCESS (ACCESS129)](methods\u002fACCESS129.html)** is a targeted 129-gene cell-free DNA\u003cbr\u003e(cfDNA) sequencing panel for plasma circulating tumor DNA profiling. The assay uses\u003cbr\u003eultra-deep coverage (~18,000\u201320,000\u00d7 raw; ~1,100\u20131,500\u00d7 duplex consensus) and includes\u003cbr\u003eSNV\u002findel calling, copy-number alterations, and structural variant detection,\u003cbr\u003eanalytically validated to 92% sensitivity at \u22650.5% VAF and \u226599.7% specificity.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**How paired normal (WBC) sequencing improves mutation calling:**\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Removes &gt;10,000 germline and clonal hematopoiesis confounders** \u2014\u003cbr\u003e[PMID:34145282](papers\u002f34145282.html) showed that plasma-only filtering plus\u003cbr\u003edatabase\u002fpopulation filtering left 10,053 confounding variants (mean VAF 4.7%), but\u003cbr\u003ematched\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=4 cite=5 \u00b7 7.7s\u003cbr\u003e# MSK-ACCESS: Overview and Design\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**MSK-ACCESS** (Memorial Sloan Kettering - Analysis of Circulating cfDNA to Examine\u003cbr\u003eSomatic Status) is an NGS assay designed to detect very low-frequency somatic alterations\u003cbr\u003ein circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) from blood plasma. The assay targets 129\u003cbr\u003ecancer-associated genes and detects multiple classes of genomic alterations including\u003cbr\u003esingle nucleotide variants (SNVs), indels, copy number alterations, and structural\u003cbr\u003evariants (PMID:34145282).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Analytical Performance\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eMSK-ACCESS demonstrates high sensitivity and specificity:\u003cbr\u003e- **92% sensitivity** for de novo mutation calling down to 0.5% allele frequency\u003cbr\u003e- **99% sensitivity** for a priori mutation profiling\u003cbr\u003e- Ultra-deep sequencing coverage of 12,000\u201325,000\u00d7 for targeted regions (PMID:34145282)\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Role of Paired Normal Sequencing\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eMatched white blood cell (WBC) DNA sequencing substantially improves sp\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD13 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is the high-intensity cfDNA + matched-WBC sequencing approach of Razavi et al., and\u003cbr\u003ewhat did it reveal about the sources of plasma cell-free DNA variants?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 10.1s\u003cbr\u003eNow let me search for the Razavi paper specifically:The [Razavi et al.\u003cbr\u003estudy](papers\u002f31768066.html) presents a high-intensity cfDNA sequencing approach paired\u003cbr\u003ewith matched white-blood-cell (WBC) sequencing to accurately distinguish tumor-derived\u003cbr\u003evariants from clonal hematopoiesis (CH). It pools\u003cbr\u003elongitudinal genomic datasets from patients treated at institutions worldwide to overcome\u003cbr\u003elogistical challenges in constructing adequately powered studies (PMID:31748746). Let me provide you with a comprehensive answer based on this source.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## The Hidden-Genome Classifier\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe **Hidden-Genome Classifier** is a novel supervised machine-learning approach\u003cbr\u003eintroduced in the cholangiocarcinoma study by [Song et al.\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:38864854)](papers\u002f38864854.html) to quantify and stratify the genetic heterogeneity\u003cbr\u003eof intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (IHC).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### What It Does\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe classifier scores each intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma tumor&#x27;s genetic\u003cbr\u003esimilarity to two reference dise\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=5 cite=5 \u00b7 6.0s\u003cbr\u003e# The Hidden-Genome Classifier\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe hidden-genome classifier is a supervised machine learning\u2013based algorithm designed to\u003cbr\u003equantify genetic heterogeneity in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (IHC) by classifying\u003cbr\u003etumors based on their genetic similarity to other biliary and liver cancers\u003cbr\u003e(PMID:38864854).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## How It Works\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe algorithm integrates comprehensive genetic meta-feature data, including:\u003cbr\u003e- Common and rare genetic variants\u003cbr\u003e- Mutational context (trinucleotide patterns)\u003cbr\u003e- Copy-number variations (CNVs)\u003cbr\u003e- Gene fusions\u003cbr\u003e- Total mutation burden\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThese complex data are synthesized into high-dimensional vectors and used to classify\u003cbr\u003eeach IHC tumor (PMID:38864854).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Key Application\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe classifier generates a numerical output called a &quot;**biliary score**&quot; for\u003cbr\u003eeach tumor, which quantifies its genetic similarity to extrahepatic biliary tumors (EHC,\u003cbr\u003eGBC) versus hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Here\u003cbr\u003eare the key definitions and findings:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### TMB Definition\u003cbr\u003e**TMB = non-synonymous somatic mutations per megabase (mut\u002fMb)** of exonic DNA sequenced,\u003cbr\u003equantified using the MSK-IMPACT targeted NGS panel (~341\u2013468 cancer-related genes\u003cbr\u003ecovering ~3% of the coding exome with matched normal sequencing to filter true somatic\u003cbr\u003evariants).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### Predictive Model for ICI Outcome\u003cbr\u003e- **High-TMB definition:** Top 20th percentile *within each histology* (not a universal\u003cbr\u003eabsolute cutpoint)\u003cbr\u003e- **Survival benefit:** Patients with high TMB had **HR 0.52 (95% CI 0.42\u20130.64)** for\u003cbr\u003eoverall survival (p = 1.6 \u00d7 10\u207b\u2076) across 1,662 ICI-treated patients\u003cbr\u003e- **ICI-specific:** The OS benefit was *not* se\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=4 cite=5 \u00b7 7.0s\u003cbr\u003e# TMB as a Survival Biomarker After Immune Checkpoint Blockade\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Definition\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eAccording to Samstein et al., tumor mutational burden (TMB) is defined as **the total\u003cbr\u003enumber of somatic non-synonymous mutations normalized to the total number of megabases\u003cbr\u003esequenced** (PMID:30643254). which\u003cbr\u003ehistotypes are examined:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Clinical Definition\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e**Radiation-associated sarcoma (RAS)** is defined as a malignant sarcoma that develops in\u003cbr\u003etissue previously exposed to therapeutic radiation, typically with a latency period\u003cbr\u003ebetween radiation exposure and sarcoma diagnosis. In the [MSK\u003cbr\u003estudy](papers\u002f37350195.html), median latencies varied by histotype: RT-AS 8.0 years,\u003cbr\u003eRT-MPNST 12.5 years, RT-UPS 18.5 years, and RT-OS 9.0 years (P = 0.0047).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Histotypes Examined\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe corpus examines **four main radiation-associated sarcoma histotypes**:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **[Radiation-associated angiosarcoma (RT-AS)](cancer_types\u002fANGS.html)** \u2014 44 cases (38\u003cbr\u003efrom breast\u002fchest wall), defin\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=4 cite=5 \u00b7 5.6s\u003cbr\u003e# Clinical Definition and Histotypes of Radiation-Associated Sarcomas\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Clinical Definition\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eRadiation-associated sarcomas are secondary malignancies that develop as a late\u003cbr\u003ecomplication of radiation therapy (RT). They are defined by a minimum time interval of at\u003cbr\u003eleast 2 years between radiation exposure and sarcoma onset (PMID:37350195). Although\u003cbr\u003eRT-associated sarcomas are rare in patients who received RT (&lt; 1%), they account for\u003cbr\u003eapproximately 5% of all sarcomas and represent &quot;a heterogeneous group of highly\u003cbr\u003eaggressive mesenchymal neoplasms associated with various histologies and clinical\u003cbr\u003epresentations&quot; (PMID:37350195).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Histotypes Examined\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe study examined the four most common RT-associated sarcoma histotypes:\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e1. **Radiation-Associated Angiosarcoma (RT-AS)**: 44 cases (54% of cohort), predominantly\u003cbr\u003efrom breast\u002fchest wall (38 cases from breast)\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e2. **Radiation-Associated Malignan\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD10 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is the RADCURE dataset, how large is it, and what makes it distinctive compared with\u003cbr\u003eearlier public HNSCC imaging resources?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=4 cite=4 \u00b7 12.6s\u003cbr\u003eLet me search for the RADCURE dataset specifically.Now let me read the primary\u003cbr\u003epublication for more details about what makes RADCURE distinctive.Based on the corpus\u003cbr\u003einformation, I can now provide you with a comprehensive answer about the RADCURE dataset.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## RADCURE Dataset Summary\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e[RADCURE](datasets\u002fradcure.html) is a large open-source head and neck cancer CT imaging\u003cbr\u003edataset comprising **3,346 patients** treated at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in\u003cbr\u003eToronto, Canada. It was published by [Welch et al. 2024](papers\u002f38362943.html).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e### Size &amp; Composition\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe dataset includes:\u003cbr\u003e- **3,346 HNSC patients** with radiation therapy simulation CT scans\u003cbr\u003e- Manually generated and quality-assured target volumes (gross primary tumor, gross nodal\u003cbr\u003evolumes) and **19 organs-at-risk contours** in DICOM RT-STRUCT format\u003cbr\u003e- Linked clinical metadata including demographics, staging (7th edition TNM), and longit\u2026\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eRAG\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=5 comp=4 cite=4 \u00b7 7.1s\u003cbr\u003e# The RADCURE Dataset\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Overview and Size\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eRADCURE is &quot;one of the most extensive head and neck cancer (HNC) imaging datasets\u003cbr\u003eaccessible to the public&quot; (PMID:38362943). It encompasses data from **3,346\u003cbr\u003epatients** featuring computed tomography (CT) radiation therapy simulation images with\u003cbr\u003ecorresponding target and organ-at-risk contours (PMID:38362943).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e## Dataset Composition\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe dataset includes:\u003cbr\u003e- **CT imaging**: Collected using systems from three different manufacturers following\u003cbr\u003estandard clinical protocols\u003cbr\u003e- **Contours**: Manually generated and reviewed at weekly radiation therapy quality\u003cbr\u003eassurance rounds, standardized to include the gross primary tumor, gross nodal volumes,\u003cbr\u003eand 19 organs-at-risk (PMID:38362943)\u003cbr\u003e- **Clinical data**: Demographics, clinical staging (7th edition TNM), and treatment\u003cbr\u003einformation linked to outcomes data with a median 5-year follow-up (60% survival rate) (\u2026","\u003cb\u003eD17 \u00b7 definition\u003c\u002fb\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eQ:\u003c\u002fb\u003e What is the Gounder et al. comprehensive sarcoma genomic profiling cohort\u003cbr\u003e(sarcoma_msk_2022), and what did profiling 7,494 sarcomas reveal about actionability?\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cb\u003eAgentic\u003c\u002fb\u003e acc=4 comp=4 cite=5 \u00b7 3.6s\u003cbr\u003eThe [Gounder et al. comprehensive sarcoma genomic profiling cohort\u003cbr\u003e(sarcoma_msk_2022)](datasets\u002fsarcoma_msk_2022.html) comprises **7,494 soft tissue and\u003cbr\u003ebone sarcomas** across 44 histologies, profiled using FoundationOne Heme (465-gene panel\u003cbr\u003e+ RNA-seq) from 2012\u20132018. \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eProfiling revealed substantial actionability opportunities:\u003cbr\u003e- **31.7%** (2,372\u002f7,494) harbored \u22651 OncoKB-actionable alteration\u003cbr\u003e- **10.5%** showed diagnostic reclassification potential\u003cbr\u003e- **TP53 pathway** altered in 47.8%; ### Figure 3 — Cost vs quality

Cost here is deliberately not budget-matched: each strategy carries its
own shape. The left panel shows input-token cost (log scale) against
total judge score; the right panel shows the same against wall time. A
well-behaved retrieval strategy should have its high-scoring dots
concentrated at the left of each panel.

![Figure 3. Total judge score vs input tokens (log scale, left) and wall
time (right), all three modes overlaid. Hybrid and RAG cluster cheap and
fast; agentic spends one-to-two orders of magnitude more to reach a
comparable score band.](plots/cost_quality.png)

*Takeaway — hybrid (≈3k tokens) and RAG (≈12k) form a tight, cheap, fast
cluster; agentic fans out to ≈280k tokens and ~3× the wall time. All three
reach the high score band on easy lookup/definition questions, so that spend
only pays off on the multi-document questions where the agent's completeness
edge lives.*

### Run guardrails

- **Agentic**: 1 / 48 runs hit the 180 s wall-clock timeout; 1 hit the 20-call tool cap.
- **Hybrid**: 0 / 48 runs hit the 180 s wall-clock timeout; 0 hit the 20-call tool cap.
- **Rag**: 0 / 48 runs hit the 180 s wall-clock timeout; 0 hit the 20-call tool cap.

Exceeding either cap is a harness-level failure, not a judge failure; the
record is kept and scored on whatever partial output was emitted before
the cap fired.

## Discussion and next steps

The held-out test split is the headline result. **Accuracy is a near-wash**
across all three modes — a single-paper factoid is roughly as answerable from
packed passages as from a graph walk. Where the agent separates is
*completeness* and *citation recall*, and only in the **enumeration-heavy
categories** (*list*, *synthesis*): reading whole pages beats passage-packing
when the answer must enumerate a set. That lead is bought with roughly an
order of magnitude more input tokens and approximately twice the wall time,
and **RAG matches the agent on accuracy while edging it on citation
correctness** at a small fraction of the cost. **Hybrid** is the cheapest and
fastest mode but trails on quality on this question set; its one-hop graph leg
does not recover the agent's completeness edge. The conclusion is therefore
one of *no free lunch*: the agent is preferable when completeness or recall on
multi-document questions justifies the cost, and dense RAG when
accuracy-per-unit-cost is the priority.

Because all three modes index the same 377 papers, these differences are
attributable to retrieval strategy rather than corpus coverage; the comparison
is controlled in that respect.

Several caveats bound how far to push the result. It rests on a single corpus
(377 papers), a single 80-question set, a single judge model, and no
statistical-significance testing on the metric differences. The RAG and hybrid
hyperparameters (chunk size, overlap, top-k, BM25 weighting, reranker, and
embedding model) were not swept; sensible defaults were used throughout. The
agent also benefits from a wiki that was itself authored by language models
from the same paper corpus, so part of its completeness advantage may derive
from that pre-processing rather than from graph-walk retrieval per se;
separating the two would require a dedicated ablation.

**Next steps, in rough priority order:**

1. **GraphRAG-style community summarization** on our wiki's cross-link
   graph ([Edge 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)). The hybrid mode already uses a thin
   one-hop graph leg; running Leiden over `wiki/graph.json` and generating
   theme-level community summaries would give the graph signal real
   synthesis depth — and address our current lack of theme pages, which the
   synthesis-category numbers suggest is where retrieval is weakest.

2. **Adaptive retrieval** — layering a reflection-token style decision
   ([Asai 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511)) or a retrieval evaluator
   ([Yan 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884)) on top of the RAG/hybrid path so it can fall through to
   graph-walk only when the top-k is weak — buying the agent's completeness
   edge without paying its token cost on every query.

3. **Corpus expansion.** This study covers 377 of cBioPortal's published
   studies. Extending to the remaining several hundred would test whether the
   category-specific agentic advantage holds, grows, or washes out with corpus
   depth.

4. **Question-set scale and judges.** A larger, possibly partially
   auto-generated question set; multiple judge models and bootstrap
   confidence intervals on every delta.

5. **Authoring themes and community pages.** A structural gap in the
   current wiki: no pre-written cross-paper synthesis pages. Their
   absence probably hurts both modes, but the agent more (it's the
   natural top-down landing page).

## References

### Seminal RAG

- Guu, K. et al. (2020). *REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training*. ICML. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08909](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08909) — Pre-trains retrieval directly into the language model via masked LM signal.
- Lewis, P. et al. (2020). *Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks*. NeurIPS. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) — Founding paper of the RAG paradigm — dense retriever + seq2seq generator.
- Izacard, G. and Grave, E. (2021). *Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering*. EACL. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01282](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01282) — Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) architecture — encodes passages independently, fuses them in the decoder.
- Izacard, G. et al. (2022). *Atlas: Few-shot Learning with Retrieval Augmented Language Models*. JMLR. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03299](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03299) — End-to-end pretrained RAG — Contriever + FiD trained jointly at scale.

### Dense retrieval and evaluation

- Karpukhin, V. et al. (2020). *Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering*. EMNLP. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906) — DPR — dual-encoder dense retrievers, the canonical RAG retriever baseline.
- Thakur, N. et al. (2021). *BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models*. NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663) — 18 diverse IR tasks — the standard benchmark for retriever robustness.
- Santhanam, K., Khattab, O. et al. (2022). *ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction*. NAACL. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488) — Token-level late interaction at cross-encoder quality, 6-10x smaller footprint.
- Es, S. et al. (2023). *RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation*. arXiv. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217) — Reference-free RAG metrics — context precision/recall, faithfulness, answer relevancy.
- Muennighoff, N. et al. (2023). *MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark*. EACL. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316) — 56+ embedding tasks across retrieval, classification, clustering; de facto embedding leaderboard.

### GraphRAG and knowledge-graph retrieval

- Edge, D. et al. (2024). *From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization*. arXiv (Microsoft Research). [https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130) — Entity KG + Leiden communities + hierarchical summaries; large gains on global sensemaking queries.
- Gao, Z. et al. (2024). *StructRAG: Boosting Knowledge Intensive Reasoning via Inference-time Hybrid Information Structurization*. arXiv. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08815](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08815) — LLM router picks per-query structure (table / graph / catalogue); beats vanilla RAG on CS + science corpora.
- Guo, Z. et al. (2024). *LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation*. EMNLP Findings. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05779](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05779) — Lightweight KG with dual-level entity + theme retrieval; ~30% latency drop vs GraphRAG.
- Gutiérrez, B. J., Shu, Y., Jiménez, E. et al. (2024). *HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models*. NeurIPS. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831) — KG + Personalized PageRank inspired by hippocampal indexing; strong on multi-hop QA at 10-30x lower cost than iterative RAG.

### Agentic retrieval and tool use

- Nakano, R. et al. (2022). *WebGPT: Browser-assisted Question-Answering with Human Feedback*. arXiv (OpenAI). [https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332) — Fine-tuned GPT-3 browses the web and cites sources; early LLM-agent milestone.
- Asai, A. et al. (2023). *Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection*. ICLR 2024. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511) — Reflection tokens let the model decide when to retrieve and critique its own outputs.
- Yao, S. et al. (2023). *ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models*. ICLR. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Interleaved reasoning traces and tool calls — the canonical agent-loop pattern.
- Yan, S.-Q. et al. (2024). *Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation*. arXiv. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884) — Retrieval evaluator triggers refinement or web-search fallback — robustness against bad retrievals.
- Singh, A. et al. (2025). *Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG*. arXiv. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09136](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09136) — 2025 survey of agentic-RAG systems — autonomous agents replacing static pipelines.

### Biomedical question-answering benchmarks

- Jin, Q. et al. (2019). *PubMedQA: A Dataset for Biomedical Research Question Answering*. EMNLP. [https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06146](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06146) — PubMed-abstract QA, yes/no format; canonical biomedical QA benchmark.
- Wadden, D. et al. (2020). *Fact or Fiction: Verifying Scientific Claims*. EMNLP. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974) — SciFact — retrieval + abstractive evidence over biomedical literature.
- Krithara, A. et al. (2023). *BioASQ-QA: A Manually Curated Corpus for Biomedical Question Answering*. Nature Scientific Data. [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02068-4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02068-4) — Curated biomedical QA — factoid / list / yes-no / summary types, annual shared task.

### D. Notable failures

Questions where either mode scored ≤ 2 on accuracy:

- **D14** (agentic, definition) — acc=2 comp=2 cite=1
  - _Judge:_ The answer appears to conflate the original 2019 GLASS paper (PMID 31748746) with a later GLASS study (likely the 2023 single-cell paper). The gold standard describes 222 patients with longitudinal DNA sequencing establishing that diagnosis drivers are retained at recurrence, alkylator therapy drives subtype-dependent hypermutation, and strongest selection acts early. The answer instead describes 304 patients, convergent recurrence phenotypes (neuronal/mesenchymal/proliferative), OSM/OSMR axes, and neuronal signaling—findings from a different publication. Key gold-standard conclusions (drivers retained, strongest selection early, subtype-dependent hypermutation) are mostly absent or only partially covered. No PMIDs are cited despite the gold PMID being 31748746.
- **D14** (rag, definition) — acc=0 comp=0 cite=4

Please go to Plans & Billing to upgrade or purchase credits.'}, 'request_id': 'req_011CbpNyzqHFaHU57CzfLJSG'}
- **L01** (hybrid, lookup) — acc=2 comp=2 cite=5
  - _Judge:_ The answer fails to provide the key fact (~3%, 204/5957 LUAD patients) and instead claims the information is not available in the retrieved passages. While it correctly cites PMID 39506116 and mentions SETD2 and LUAD, it does not answer the question, representing a significant gap in completeness and an effectively wrong/missing answer.
- **L06** (hybrid, lookup) — acc=2 comp=3 cite=5
  - _Judge:_ The answer cites the correct PMID and references the correct trial, but reports the 1-year PFS as 75% for a subgroup not treated with salvage therapy, rather than the overall 1-year PFS of 61.7% which is the key finding. This is a significant factual error regarding the primary endpoint result, and the comparison to the historical control (43.8%, log-rank P=0.002) is missing.
- **L09** (agentic, lookup) — acc=2 comp=3 cite=5
  - _Judge:_ The answer incorrectly identifies NRAS as the co-driver with KRAS for the mucinous subtype. The gold answer specifies KRAS and GNAS as the two RAS-pathway genes that co-drive the mucinous subtype. While GNAS is mentioned in the answer, it is incorrectly described as being absent in this subtype rather than being a co-driver. The citation is correct.
- **L16** (agentic, lookup) — acc=1 comp=1 cite=1
  - _Judge:_ The answer fails to provide the correct percentage (89%) and cites the wrong PMID (31061129 instead of 26000489). The gold standard refers to the Robinson et al. 2015 study, not the Abida et al. 2019 study. The answer is fundamentally wrong on the key fact and uses an incorrect citation.
- **LS03** (agentic, list) — acc=2 comp=1 cite=1
